alt: “The streets were choked with traffic” read in two layers. Its meaning is that the streets were very crowded; its effect is that “choked” makes the city seem to struggle to breathe, as if strangled, so the reader senses discomfort and something close to danger. Meaning alone answers Question 1; Question 2 rewards effect.
caption: Question 2 rewards the second layer: what the word choice makes the reader see or feel.

alt: House and home can denote the same building, but home carries warmth, belonging and family. “She walked”, “drifted” and “stormed” into the room describe the same action, yet each verb gives a different character and mood.
caption: Effects come from what a word brings with it beyond its dictionary meaning.

alt: Three steps beside the worked answer on “sagged”: quote precisely, explain the meaning or image (bodies collapsing under their own weight) and explain the effect in context (the people have lost all their energy, which shows how long they have waited).
caption: Quote, explain the image, then say what it does in this moment of the text.

alt: For a three-mark question on the station extract, each of the last three sentences gives one choice: the simile “like a hand” makes the heat physical and heavy, the broken rhythm of the baby’s wail mirrors endless noise, and “swallowed” shows information lost and travellers helpless. Each feature with its effect earns one mark.
caption: In a three-mark question, choose three different features, each with its own effect.

alt: Four sentence shapes and their typical effects: a very short sentence after long ones gives a sudden stop, shock or emphasis; a long list sentence suggests abundance, chaos or breathlessness; repetition at the start of clauses gives insistence and rhythm; a question suggests doubt or a character’s inner voice.
caption: Sentence form is language too; explain what its shape does here.

alt: Four stock phrases, such as “it makes the reader want to read on” and “it creates a vivid image”, are crossed out because they fit any text. The replacement names the specific picture: the reader pictures people collapsing like emptied sacks.
caption: If a sentence about effect could fit any text, replace it with the picture this text creates.
